n: A dated message: the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year—about January 588 BC. This very day the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem began, hundreds of miles away.

f.w: in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day

n: Ezekiel must write the date down. When news later arrives, the exiles will know God revealed it to him on the exact day. Jews still fast on the tenth of Tevet to remember it.

f.w: write thee the name of the day
f.g: Record the date as evidence of true prophecy.

n: Another parable for the rebellious house: put a pot on the fire and pour in water. This recalls the leaders’ boast that Jerusalem was a safe “caldron” (11:3).
Fill it with the best cuts—thigh and shoulder—and choice bones. These represent Jerusalem’s leading citizens.
Use the best of the flock, pile wood underneath, and boil it hard until even the bones are cooked—the siege will be intense.
Woe to the bloody city, a pot crusted with rust (“scum”) that won’t come off. Empty it piece by piece without casting lots—no one will be chosen to be spared.

f.g: Probably rust or corrosion—a picture of deep-set guilt.

f.w: let no lot fall upon it
f.g: No selection; all will be removed.

n: Jerusalem’s bloodshed is exposed on bare rock, not covered with dust as the law required for spilled blood. Her violence is open and unashamed.
So God has left her blood uncovered, crying out for justice.

f.w: that it should not be covered

n: Woe to the bloody city! God himself will build the woodpile high.
Pile on wood, light the fire, cook the meat well, and let the bones burn. Judgment will be thorough.

f.g: Possibly “boil it down” or “mix in spices.”

n: Then set the empty pot on the coals until the bronze glows hot and the rust burns away. Even purging the city itself becomes necessary.

f.w: that the filthiness of it may be molten in it

n: All the effort has failed; her heavy rust won’t come off. It must go into the fire.

f.w: She hath wearied herself with lies
f.g: Or “it has wearied all efforts”—the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: God tried to cleanse her through earlier warnings, but she refused to be cleansed. Now she won’t be clean until his anger is spent.

f.w: because I have purged thee, and thou wast not purged

n: God has spoken and will act; he won’t turn back or relent. Their own deeds will be their judges.

f.g: Neither will I change my mind.

n: Another message—one of the most personal moments in all the prophets.

f.w: Also the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: The following sign costs Ezekiel deeply.

n: God tells Ezekiel he is about to take away “the desire of his eyes”—his beloved wife—suddenly. Yet he must not mourn publicly or weep.

f.g: The one he loved most—his wife (v. 18).

n: He may groan silently but must not perform the customary mourning rites: he keeps his turban and sandals on, doesn’t cover his face, and doesn’t eat the meal neighbors bring to mourners.

f.w: bind the tire of thine head upon thee
f.g: Keep your turban on, rather than baring your head in grief.
Covering the lower face was a sign of mourning.
The meal friends brought to a grieving family.

n: Ezekiel spoke to the people in the morning; that evening his wife died. The next morning he obeyed. His quiet obedience in deep grief is one of the most moving moments in the book.

f.g: The only mention of Ezekiel’s wife.

f.w: I did in the morning as I was commanded

n: Puzzled that he isn’t mourning, the people ask what it means for them.
Ezekiel explains God’s message.

f.w: The word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: His silence was a message from God.

n: God will profane his sanctuary—the temple that is Israel’s pride, the delight of their eyes, the object of their deepest longing. Their children left in Jerusalem will die by the sword.

f.g: The same phrase used for Ezekiel’s wife (v. 16).

n: When the news comes, they will react as Ezekiel did—without the usual mourning rituals.

f.w: ye shall do as I have done
f.g: Their loss will be too overwhelming for normal mourning.

n: They will not weep openly but will waste away because of their sins and groan to one another. Shock and guilt will leave them numb.

f.w: ye shall pine away for your iniquities

n: Ezekiel himself is the sign. When it happens, they will know the Lord. This is the only place the prophet’s name appears outside chapter 1.

f.w: Ezekiel is unto you a sign

n: On the day God takes away their stronghold, their joy and glory, the delight of their eyes, and their children…

f.w: that whereupon they set their minds

n: …a survivor will escape and bring the news to Ezekiel.
On that day Ezekiel’s silence will end; he will speak freely again. The fulfillment comes in 33:21–22, when a refugee reports “The city is fallen.”
